newsitem.title: USA: Debit cards -- debit with care.
newsitem.headline: Debit cards -- debit with care.

text.p: By the time you read this, there's a good chance your bank has either sent you a new debit card or notified you of its intention to send you one, probably to serve you better.

Why? Bankers love the new plastic, which looks like a credit card but acts like a check. And why shouldn't they? Debit cards enable bankers to reduce the number of paper checks they handle and collect fees from the merchants who accept them.

It's not so simple to understand why consumers have taken to the plastic checks, but checking account customers have racked up more than $50 million on these plastic checks, almost all of which sport Mastercard or Visa logos.

Bring it to a store, and the clerk will process you through in a flash, just as if you were paying with a regular credit card. But the totals will be deducted from your checking account almost as quickly, so forget about float.
Should you adopt a "have debit card, will travel" approach? Yes and no.

If you use them correctly, they can be a convenience, but first learn the rules. There are two types of debit transactions and both are often housed in the same card, which may be the new one your bank sent you as a replacement for your old ATM card.

Online transactions are the kind you perform at a cash machine. For an online transaction, you need to use a personal identification number (PIN) and the funds you tap are electronically transferred from your checking account within moments.

That's your typical ATM or grocery store debit card transaction, and it ain't free. Use your card for an online transaction at the grocery or gas station, and you can be hit with fees as high as 50 cents per use.
If you use your card online like a traditional bank card at an ATM machine that doesn't belong to your bank, your fees for getting cash back can go as high as $3 per transaction.
But what's new and growing faster than these transactions are the so-called "offline transactions."
These feel like credit card sales and don't require PINs. The store clerk may not even know you are using a debit card and not a credit card.

The total will get subtracted from your checking account within a day or two or three, but not within moments. And typically, you won't pay a fee for the transaction, although the merchant will kick about 3 percent back to the bank for the privilege of using the card.
What's the moral? Go for the offline transactions, which buy you time and convenience and don't cost you much. Limit your use of online transactions.

Is it really worth a quarter or 50 cents just to not write a check at the grocery? And be careful at the gas station: Some charge more for credit than they do for cash. And even though your debit card spends like cash, it looks like credit.

Finally, be careful how you carry the card. They are as easy to steal as a credit card, but the results are much more painful. A thief with your debit card (or just your debit card number!) can clean out your checking account before you figure out that anything's missing, said Ruth Susswein of the Bankcard Holders of America.

Paper checks you've written can bounce while you are sorting it all out with your bank, and that sorting process can turn nasty if your banker doesn't believe you or takes too long to replace missing money.

If you report a lost or stolen card to the bank within two business days, your liability is limited to $50, but if you wait longer than that, your liability goes up to $500. If you don't discover the theft until you get your checking account statement, you have 60 days to report it and limit your liability to $50.
